topic: repairing a worn leather satchel with workshop tools and saddle stitching

provenance.author: glowny-en-d
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is seam, thread and rivet arithmetic on the same repair with closed task questions, base is a repair dialogue about a torn strap and rotten seams. Grounded external referent: the stitching clamp, introduced in turn 0 (it holds the work throughout) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion.

a: Here is the repair sheet for one leather satchel, with five seams that need restitching in order.
The gusset seam on the left runs twelve inches, and the right gusset runs the same twelve.
The flap seam runs nine inches, and the strap join needs a double row of four inches each.
The base seam is the longest single run at fourteen inches from corner to corner.
How many inches of seam does the whole repair come to across all five lines?
base: My leather satchel has come apart along the front strap, and the tear runs into the flap.
The stitching on the gusset has rotted too, so whole seams pull open when the bag is lifted.
I hold the work in an old wooden clamp between my knees, the way my grandfather did.
The leather itself still feels sound, though the surface has gone dull and dry in places.
Where should I begin so that I do not make the damage worse than it already is?

a: The two gussets together make twenty-four inches, and the flap brings the total to thirty-three.
The strap join adds eight inches over its two rows, taking the count to forty-one.
The base seam adds fourteen more inches, so the whole repair comes to fifty-five inches in all.
At eight stitches to the inch, the five seams need four hundred forty stitches in all.
Does the fifty-five inch total agree with the figure written on the repair sheet?
base: Begin by unpicking the rotten seams completely, because half-removed thread will foul every new stitch you set.
Save the old thread ends and count the holes, since the original spacing tells you the stitch length.
Flex the gusset gently, as dry leather can crack the moment it is folded back.
Keep the clamp jaws padded with scrap, so the wood does not bruise the damp grain.
Does the tear by the buckle go through the strap, or only through the top layer?

a: Now work out the thread, cutting each length at four times the seam it will close.
List the five thread lengths in the same order as the seams on the sheet.
Round every length up to the next whole inch before it goes on the list.
Thread comes off a single spool holding twelve yards ready on the bench.
Which single thread length belongs to the strap join under that fixed rule of four?
base: The tear goes right through the strap, about a thumb's width below the buckle fold.
The clamp holds the strap steady, but the loose end flaps about while I work.
I have unpicked one gusset seam already, and the holes underneath look clean and evenly spaced.
There are eight holes to the inch along the seam, as far as I can tell.
Should I cut the strap back to solid leather, or patch across the torn part instead?

a: Each gusset seam takes forty-eight inches of thread, and the flap seam takes thirty-six.
The strap join takes sixteen inches per row, which makes thirty-two across its two rows.
The base seam takes fifty-six inches, the longest single length on the whole list.
The five lengths together come to two hundred twenty inches, or just over six yards.
Does the spool of twelve yards cover the two hundred twenty inches with room to spare?
base: Cut back to solid leather every time, because a patch over a tear only moves the strain along.
Make the new strap piece overlap the old by a good hand's width for the join.
Set the join in the clamp and stitch two parallel rows through both layers.
Use the old holes where you can, and prick new ones only past the torn section.
Do you have thread that is waxed, or shall we talk about waxing it yourself?

a: One correction before the cutting starts, because the base seam was measured wrong on the sheet.
The base seam is sixteen inches, not fourteen, so its stitch count and thread must change.
Recalculate the seam total, the stitch total and the base thread length with the new figure.
Leave the four other seams exactly as they stand on the list already.
What does the base seam thread length become at four times sixteen inches?
base: I have a spool of unwaxed linen thread and a small block of beeswax from the market.
One correction to what I said before, because I measured the seam again this morning.
The gusset runs nine holes to the inch, not eight, so my earlier count was wrong.
The clamp jaws sit a little proud of the seam, which makes the awl angle awkward.
Does the finer spacing change the thread thickness I should be using for the rows?

a: The seam total rises from fifty-five to fifty-seven inches with the corrected base figure.
The stitch count rises to four hundred fifty-six at eight stitches to the inch.
The base thread length becomes sixty-four inches under the fixed rule of four times.
The full thread requirement is now two hundred twenty-eight inches across the five seams.
Does the new thread total still sit inside the twelve yard spool as it did before?
base: Finer spacing does call for thinner thread, or the holes will tear into one another.
Draw each length through the beeswax three or four times until it hangs stiff.
Cut lengths of about four times the seam, since a saddle stitch eats thread from both sides.
Lower the work in the clamp so the seam sits just above the jaws.
Have you got two needles, because the stitch needs one on each end of the thread?

a: Next count the hardware, because the buckle end needs rivets as well as stitching.
The strap join takes four rivets, and each corner of the base takes one more.
Rivets come in boxes of ten, and only full boxes can be ordered from the supplier.
Add two spare rivets to the count in case any head splits when it is set.
How many boxes does the order need once the spares are counted in?
base: I have two harness needles, and I have waxed three lengths of thread as you described.
The first row along the strap join went in slowly but it looks tight and even.
The edges of the flap are still ragged where the old stitching chewed them up.
I would like the finished bag to look cared for rather than merely held together.
What should I do with the raw edges once the seams are all closed again?

a: The join and the corners together take eight rivets before any spares are added.
With the two spares the count comes to ten rivets exactly for the whole job.
Ten rivets fill one box of ten, so the order is a single full box.
Nothing is left in the box if both spares are used at the setting stage.
Is one box the figure that goes onto the order form for the supplier?
base: Trim the ragged edges back with a sharp knife held flat against the grain.
Damp the cut edge lightly and rub it down with a slicker until it shines.
A coat of edge paint or plain wax will keep the fibres from lifting again.
Work in thin coats and let each one dry before the next goes on.
Is the bag kept dry at home, or does it ride in the rain a lot?

a: Now set out the whole job in four evening sessions, with one evening given to each session.
Session one is unpicking, session two is cutting, and session three is the stitching.
Session four is the riveting and the edge work, which close the job out.
The stitching evening must cover four hundred fifty-six stitches at a pace of two stitches a minute.
That pace puts the stitching at two hundred twenty-eight minutes of steady work.
base: The bag rides to work on a bicycle, so it does see rain most weeks.
I will finish the seams tonight and slick the edges over the weekend as you suggest.
After that I plan to feed the leather with a conditioning balm before it goes back into use.
It will feel good to see the old bag whole again after all these years.
The satchel belonged to my grandfather, and I want it to outlast me as well.

a: Two hundred twenty-eight minutes is three hours and forty-eight minutes of stitching time.
The unpicking evening and the cutting evening are shorter, at about two hours each.
The riveting and edge evening runs about ninety minutes with the tools laid out ready.
The four sessions together come to roughly nine hours and twenty minutes of work.
The job closes at the end of session four with every seam, rivet and edge finished.
base: Give the balm a full day to sink in before the bag carries any weight.
Wipe the buckle and rings with an oily rag so the new thread stays clean.
Check the stitch rows after the first wet week and again after the first month.
A repaired seam that survives its first month will usually survive for years after that.
Your grandfather's satchel should see many more winters on the handlebars than you expect.
